title: 1 Samuel 4:1–11
context: After a note that Samuel’s word came to all Israel, Israel fights the Philistines and is defeated; the elders bring the ark from Shiloh, with Eli’s sons Hophni and Phinehas, hoping it will save them. The Philistines are terrified but fight harder, and Israel suffers a great defeat: the ark is captured and Eli’s sons are killed. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground: God’s presence cannot be manipulated, and the judgment announced on Eli’s house begins to fall.

verses.text: The word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now Israel went out against the Philistines to battle, and encamped beside Ebenezer; and the Philistines encamped in Aphek.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The word of Samuel came to all Israel” opens the verse, and then Israel goes out to battle at Ebenezer while the Philistines camp at Aphek. Arminian readers note that the verse joins the end of Samuel’s call story with the start of the war narrative.

In engwebp, the first sentence stands in its own paragraph before the battle account begins; the locations are uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the text does not say Israel consulted God or Samuel before the battle.

The verse division falls in the middle of the narrative flow. The Septuagint has additional wording at 4:1, which is noted as a textual matter.

verses.text: The Philistines put themselves in array against Israel. When they joined battle, Israel was defeated by the Philistines, who killed about four thousand men of the army in the field.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines defeat Israel in the field and kill about four thousand men. Arminian readers note that the setback drives the elders to ask why the LORD allowed it.

The defeat raises the question that the rest of the chapter answers: God’s presence cannot be taken for granted.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s hand behind the defeat as discipline on a people led by a corrupt priesthood (1 Sam 2:12–17).

The loss forces Israel to face its spiritual condition, though the elders draw the wrong conclusion.

verses.text: When the people had come into the camp, the elders of Israel said, “Why has the LORD defeated us today before the Philistines? Let’s get the ark of the LORD’s covenant out of Shiloh and bring it to us, that it may come among us and save us out of the hand of our enemies.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The elders ask why the LORD defeated them and decide to bring the ark to save them. Arminian readers note that they rightly ask why, but answer by treating the ark like a charm.

They seek a means rather than repentance (cf. Num 14:44).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see an attempt to use God’s symbol to compel his help.

Both traditions read this as a warning against treating sacred things as magic (cf. Jer 7:4, 12–14).

verses.text: So the people sent to Shiloh, and they brought from there the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Armies, who sits above the cherubim; and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.
verses.arminianNotes:
They bring the ark of the LORD of Armies, who sits above the cherubim, with Hophni and Phinehas. Arminian readers note the irony: the ark comes with the very priests under judgment.

The title stresses God’s majesty (cf. Exod 25:22; 2 Sam 6:2).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the contrast between God’s glory and the unworthy priests carrying it.

The presence of Eli’s sons signals the coming fulfillment of judgment.

verses.text: When the ark of the LORD’s covenant came into the camp, all Israel shouted with a great shout, so that the earth resounded.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the ark arrives, Israel shouts so the earth resounds. Arminian readers note the confidence placed in the ark.

Enthusiasm is not the same as faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see misplaced confidence. The shout recalls Jericho (Josh 6:20) but without obedience.

Outward religious fervor cannot replace a right heart.

verses.text: When the Philistines heard the noise of the shout, they said, “What does the noise of this great shout in the camp of the Hebrews mean?” They understood that the LORD’s ark had come into the camp.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines hear the shout and learn the ark has come. Arminian readers note that the enemy also understood the ark’s significance.

The news strikes fear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the nations’ awareness of Israel’s God.

The Philistines’ reaction prepares for their defiant resolve.

verses.text: The Philistines were afraid, for they said, “God has come into the camp.” They said, “Woe to us! For there has not been such a thing before.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines are afraid, saying, “God has come into the camp.” Arminian readers note the irony: the enemy fears God more than Israel truly trusts him.

They assume the ark brings God’s presence automatically, the same mistake Israel made.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see pagan thinking that equates God with his symbol, mirroring Israel’s own error in verse 3.

The Philistines’ fear is real but misdirected. God is present, but not as a tool for either side.

verses.text: Woe to us! Who shall deliver us out of the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods that struck the Egyptians with all kinds of plagues in the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes:
They cry, “Who shall deliver us out of the hand of these mighty gods?” and recall the plagues on Egypt. Arminian readers note that news of the exodus had spread among the nations (cf. Josh 2:10).

They speak of “gods,” showing their pagan assumptions about Israel’s God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s reputation among the nations, even if garbled.

The memory of the plagues on Egypt frames what will happen in chapter 5, where God’s hand strikes the Philistines in a way that recalls the exodus.

verses.text: Be strong and behave like men, O you Philistines, that you not be servants to the Hebrews, as they have been to you. Strengthen yourselves like men, and fight!”
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines urge each other to be strong and fight. Arminian readers note that fear drives them to greater effort.

They fight to avoid becoming servants.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see human courage at work, yet the outcome is in God’s hands.

The Philistines’ resolve will serve God’s purpose of judgment on Israel.

verses.text: The Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and each man fled to his tent. There was a very great slaughter; for thirty thousand footmen of Israel fell.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines fight, Israel is defeated, and thirty thousand footmen fall. Arminian readers note the great slaughter, far worse than the first defeat.

The ark did not save them because God’s presence cannot be manipulated by those who ignore his word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s judgment on Israel, later recalled in Psalm 78:60–62, where God abandons the tent at Shiloh.

The defeat demonstrates God’s holiness and sovereignty over his own symbols. Large numbers in these narratives are discussed by interpreters.

verses.text: God’s ark was taken; and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were slain.
verses.arminianNotes:
“God’s ark was taken; and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were slain.” Arminian readers note the fulfillment of the sign given to Eli that both sons would die on one day (1 Sam 2:34).

The deaths are recorded soberly, without comment or gloating.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s word against Eli’s house fulfilled exactly as announced (1 Sam 2:34; 3:12).

Psalm 78:61 speaks of God delivering his strength into captivity and his glory into the enemy’s hand, a sobering picture of judgment on his own people.
